reflection.quote: The unexamined life is not worth living, but the unlived life is not worth examining either.
reflection.quoteAuthor: Adapted from Socrates, via Harold Brodkey
reflection.reading:
There's a specific kind of Saturday in late July that used to disappear on me. I'd wake up around noon, already behind, already reaching for something to take the edge off the guilt of losing another one. The day would blur into evening and evening into a story I'd have to piece together on Sunday. Twenty, thirty, forty Saturdays a year, gone.

The Saturdays I have now are not always exciting. Some are — a trip somewhere, a wedding, a river. But most are ordinary. Coffee that I actually taste. A run in the heat. Laundry. A friend texting to grab lunch and me being the kind of person who shows up, on time, present, remembering what we talked about last week. This is the part nobody warned me would matter so much. The stakes of a regular Saturday are low, which is exactly why they're high. This is where a life actually gets built.

When I was 22, I thought sobriety meant losing the good parts and keeping the boring ones. It turned out to be closer to the opposite. The dull, hazy fog lifted, and underneath was a Saturday I could remember on Sunday. That's not small. That's the whole thing. The examined life, sure — but also the lived one. You need both, and you can't have either drunk.
reflection.meditation: What would it mean to be fully present for this ordinary day, exactly as it is?

affirmations: I am building a life I can remember on Sunday.
Today I show up for the small things, because that's where the real ones live.
I have agency over how I meet this day, no matter what it brings.

gratitude.prayer: Grateful for a Saturday I get to be awake for. Grateful for the people who text me knowing I'll answer, and the version of myself that's earned that trust back. Grateful for coffee I can taste, air I can breathe deep, and the quiet fact of another day on this side of it.
gratitude.closing: One ordinary, unrepeatable day. That's enough.
